title: QQ plot and residual diagnostics: are errors Gaussian and unbiased?
summary: Three views of a model's residuals: a QQ plot against a normal distribution, residuals against fitted value, and a histogram with a normal curve. Together they test the two assumptions most analyses rely on: errors are roughly Gaussian, and they have zero mean with constant spread.

media.alt: Three panels: left, a QQ plot of residual quantiles against theoretical normal quantiles with a dashed reference line, points close to it with a few above at the upper right; centre, residuals against fitted value with a dashed zero line, the spread widening slightly to the right; right, a histogram of residuals with a dashed normal curve and a dotted line at zero, title mean = -0.08.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Are errors Gaussian and unbiased?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: theoretical quantile of N(0,1) on x, sample quantile of the residuals on y. Centre: fitted value (0 to 10) on x, residual on y. Right: residual on x, density on y.
look_at: In the QQ plot, do the points follow the line in the middle and in the tails?
In the residual versus fitted panel, is the cloud centred on zero with constant width, or is there a trend or a funnel?
In the histogram, is the shape bell-like and centred on zero?
Is the reference line explained (which line, fitted how)?
as_drawn: 150 residuals. The QQ points lie on the line from about -2 to +2 and then bend: the three or four largest points are above it at the upper right, a sign of heavier-than-normal tails.

The residual panel shows no trend, but the scatter widens slightly towards large fitted values (the standard deviation grows by about 30 percent from 0 to 10), with the largest residuals near 1.7 at fitted values of 6 to 8.
The histogram has a mean of -0.08 (title) and is a little more peaked than the dashed normal curve; the dotted line at zero marks the no-bias reference.
The QQ reference line is the least-squares line through the points (slope 0.59, intercept -0.08), whose slope is the residual standard deviation and whose intercept is the mean.
read_the_figure.proves: Points on the QQ line, a flat even cloud and a centred histogram are consistent with Gaussian, unbiased errors of constant spread. They do not prove it: with 150 points only large departures are visible.
if_wrong: S-shaped QQ points: tails heavier or lighter than normal.
A funnel in the residual versus fitted panel: the spread depends on the level (heteroscedasticity); consider a transformation or weights.
A histogram not centred on zero: bias, which the zero line in the third panel should expose.
must_check: reference line: the QQ plot is a comparison, and without a line the reader cannot judge what straight means.

terms.meaning: A scatter of the sorted sample values against the quantiles of a reference distribution; a straight line means the sample has that distribution (up to location and scale).
The value of the standard normal at the plotting position (i - 0.5) / n.
A spread of the residuals that changes with the fitted value or another variable.
A measure of tail weight relative to the normal distribution; zero for a normal, positive for heavy tails.
The mean of the residuals; zero for an unbiased model.

remember: QQ line: slope = standard deviation, intercept = mean of the residuals.
Student t with 6 degrees of freedom has excess kurtosis 6 / (6 - 4) = 3.
Test the mean against its standard error: z = mean / (s / sqrt(n)).
A funnel in residual versus fitted means non-constant variance.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: each point is one residual, placed by its rank (horizontal: where a normal sample of the same size would put it) and its value (vertical); the amber dashed line is the normal reference. Centre: each point is one residual plotted against the model's fitted value, with the amber zero line. Right: a histogram of residuals with the amber dashed normal curve of the same mean and spread and the rose dotted zero line.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: most statistical methods assume errors are bell-shaped, centred and equally noisy everywhere. If the model has captured the signal, what is left should look like plain noise. The QQ plot turns 'bell-shaped' into 'lies on a straight line', which the eye can judge far better than a histogram; the residual versus fitted plot shows whether the noise depends on the level; the histogram shows the centre and the shape.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: QQ plots of small samples always wiggle, and the tails move most; a few points off the line at the ends are not necessarily a problem. The bins of the histogram change its appearance. A mean of -0.08 looks like a bias but its standard error is 0.048, so it is 1.7 standard errors from zero and not significant. A good-looking residual plot does not show that the model is right, only that it has left no obvious pattern.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A formal test (Shapiro-Wilk, Anderson-Darling) gives a p-value but not the shape of the departure. A detrended QQ plot (the difference from the line against the quantile) magnifies departures. A plot of the absolute residuals against the fitted values shows heteroscedasticity more clearly than the signed residuals.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a 95 percent envelope to the QQ plot from simulated normal samples of the same size, print the mean with its standard error on the histogram, and add a smooth line through the absolute residuals in the centre panel.

steps.title: How a QQ plot is built
steps.note: If the residuals are N(mu, sigma^2) the points lie on y = mu + sigma x: slope sigma, intercept mu.

steps.title: Tail weight
steps.note: The residuals of the render come from a t distribution with 6 degrees of freedom: heavier tails than the normal, as the bent ends of the QQ plot show. The sample value is 0.35 for 150 points; tails are hard to estimate.

steps.title: Is the mean different from zero?
steps.note: Not significant at the 5 percent level (needs |z| above 1.96).

worked.title: Reading the residual diagnostics of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What do the slope and intercept of the QQ line tell you? (2) Is the mean of -0.08 evidence of bias? (3) What does the centre panel say about the variance?

solution.text: (1) The line has slope 0.59 and intercept -0.08: the residuals have a standard deviation of about 0.59 and a mean of about -0.08.
(2) Compare the mean with its standard error.
So the mean is not significantly different from zero.
(3) The scatter widens slightly to the right: by construction the standard deviation grows as 1 + 0.03 times the fitted value, which is a factor 1.3 between 0 and 10. A mild funnel.

worked.answer: Standard deviation 0.59 and mean -0.08; z = -1.7, so no significant bias; a mild funnel (variance increasing with the fitted value) and slightly heavy tails.

analyze.q: The upper-right QQ points are above the line. What does that say about the largest residuals?
Why is it not enough to look at the histogram alone?
Which remedy would you try for a funnel in the residuals?
analyze.hint: Transform the response or weight the fit.

evaluate.q: The QQ plot is straight in the middle and bent at the ends. Do you drop the normality assumption?

create: Add a 95 percent simulation envelope to the QQ plot and print the mean with its standard error on the histogram.
Plot the absolute residuals against the fitted values with a smooth trend.

checks.q: What does a straight line in a QQ plot mean?
checks.answer: The sample has the shape of the reference distribution (up to a shift and a scale): the points follow y = mean + sd x.

checks.q: Residuals have mean -0.1, standard deviation 0.5 and n = 100. Is the mean significant?
checks.answer: SE = 0.05, z = -2.0, just beyond the 1.96 cutoff: marginally significant.

checks.q: The residual versus fitted plot is a funnel. What does it imply for the confidence intervals of the fit?
checks.answer: The intervals assume constant variance, so they are too narrow where the spread is large and too wide where it is small; use weights or transform the data.
